I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I have failed in my most important role in life
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner', the appraisal 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' is clinically hard to reconcile because this trauma does not ordinarily involve other deaths or a mass-casualty context. The rest of the profile centers on partner violence, hypervigilance, and fragmented visual recall, so this item introduces a markedly different trauma scenario without support elsewhere in the selected items.

'Car sounds' is difficult to connect clinically to the rest of this profile for physical abuse by a romantic partner. The other trigger items and all threat, memory, and appraisal items center on interpersonal trauma, bodily alarm, betrayal, and fragmented terror-based recall. A car-sound trigger suggests a different trauma context unless there is supporting material elsewhere, so this item is the main coherence concern.

vignette:
# Rajesh

Rajesh was thirty-eight when he met Marcus at a gallery opening in Brooklyn. Marcus was charming, attentive, and seemed to understand the loneliness that had settled into Rajesh's life after his parents' death. For two years, their relationship felt like rescue. Then, during an argument about money in the spring of 2021, Marcus shoved him against the kitchen counter. The shock of it—the physical betrayal by someone Rajesh had allowed into his body and home—was less about pain than about the shattering of something Rajesh had believed was solid. Over the following months, the violence escalated. Marcus would grab him by the throat, pin him to walls, once threw a glass that cut Rajesh's shoulder. What made it worse was the pattern: Marcus would apologize, promise it would never happen again, and Rajesh would believe him because he wanted to, because the alternative—admitting he had failed at the one relationship he had fought so hard to build—felt impossible. When Rajesh finally left in December, he carried with him the certainty that he could not trust his own judgment. He had missed every warning sign. He had stayed too long. He had, by some logic his mind kept returning to, deserved it.

The first symptoms appeared within weeks. Rajesh found himself unable to sleep more than four hours a night, his body rigid in bed beside his new partner, Sarah, his mind cataloging exits and potential threats. When Sarah came home from work and called out his name in a voice slightly higher than usual, Rajesh's heart would race before his conscious mind had even registered what he'd heard. A client's raised voice during a design review would send a jolt through his nervous system so acute he'd excuse himself to the bathroom. By spring, he had begun to notice that certain sensory moments—the smell of whiskey on a colleague's breath, the sound of someone speaking rapid, slurred words that he couldn't quite parse—would trigger something immediate and overwhelming. Each time these sensory cues arrived, they carried a thought with them: *I missed the signs before; I'll miss them again.* The smell of whiskey didn't just activate the memory—it told him something about himself, that his judgment was permanently compromised, that he was the kind of person who couldn't be trusted to recognize danger until it was too late. His body would react first, flooding with adrenaline, his muscles tensing as though bracing for impact, before his rational mind could catch up and tell him he was safe in his office in Manhattan, that no one was about to hurt him. The incomprehensible chatter of drunk people on the subway, the acrid smell of alcohol wafting from a bar he passed on his commute, even the sensation of coming down with a cold—these ordinary moments had become dangerous, because each one carried him back to those moments with Marcus, the terror returning with photographic clarity. He could see Marcus's face above him, could feel the pressure of hands on his chest, could smell the whiskey on his breath, and the memory arrived not as a narrative but as a series of frozen images that his mind replayed with horrifying precision.

What terrified Rajesh most was not just the memories themselves but what they meant about him. He had come to believe that his inability to see Marcus's violence coming—his failure to recognize danger, his willingness to stay—revealed something fundamentally broken in his capacity to make sound decisions. Once he had settled into this belief—that he was unreliable, damaged, incapable of protecting himself—the world began to feel actively threatening. He walked into rooms already braced, his body tensing in anticipation of danger, because he had become certain that if he could miss Marcus's violence, he could miss anything; nowhere was truly safe if he was the one responsible for detecting threat. When he felt ill, when his body began to register the early signs of flu, he would spiral into self-recrimination: *I can't trust myself to know what's real anymore.* The physical symptoms, the sensory triggers, they all fed back into his conviction that he was unreliable, that he had failed in the most important role of his life—to be a good partner, a discerning person, someone worthy of love. His body's hypervigilance, the way it would startle at the slightest unexpected sound, seemed to confirm his deepest fear: that he was damaged, that his threat detection had been broken all along, that perhaps it still was. And this belief—that he was fundamentally flawed—kept him awake at night, scanning the darkness for danger, unable to lower his guard because to do so felt like the same reckless trust that had nearly destroyed him.

Over the past year, Rajesh's avoidance had narrowed his world considerably. He stopped attending team dinners after work. He began requesting remote-only meetings, a request his firm accommodated but which marked him as difficult, unpredictable. Sarah noticed he would leave the room if she opened a bottle of wine. He could not sit in crowded bars or restaurants. The very architecture that had once brought him joy—designing open, collaborative spaces—now felt impossible to imagine inhabiting. He had come to therapy because Sarah had finally told him, with a firmness that cut through his fog, that she could not watch him disappear. What he wanted most was to trust again—to trust his instincts, his judgment, himself. What he feared most was that the person he had become—hypervigilant, doubtful, trapped in a loop of memory and threat—was permanent, that Marcus had rewritten something essential in him that could never be restored.

Negative appraisals (beliefs that he is 'fundamentally broken', 'unreliable', 'damaged') are described in paragraph 3, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that these appraisals drive or intensify the sense of threat; instead, threat responses and hypervigilance are presented as confirming the appraisals rather than being caused by them.
